case_name: Rose v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police)
text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Rose v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted
Police),

2009 BCSC 1750

Date: 20091218

Docket:
09-4428

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Jerry
Douglas Rose Jr.

Plaintiff

And:

Her
Majesty the Queen in Right of Canada as represented by the Royal Canadian
Mounted Police (Government of Canada, R.C.M.P.) and as represented by the
Attorney General of Canada and Her Majesty the Queen in Right of the Province
of British Columbia as represented by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police “E”
Division (Government of British Columbia, R.C.M.P.) and as represented by the
Ministry of

Public Safety and the Solicitor General of British Columbia

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Macaulay

Reasons for Judgment

Jerry Douglas Rose Jr.

In Person

Counsel for the Defendants:

M.F. Volk

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria, B.C.

December 8, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria, B.C.

December 18, 2009

[
1
]

The defendants apply, pursuant to Rule 19(24),
to have the plaintiff’s statement of claim struck and the proceedings
dismissed. They also apply for an order restraining the plaintiff, Mr. Rose,
from commencing or continuing any further legal proceedings in the Supreme
Court or Provincial Court of British Columbia without leave of the Supreme
Court pursuant to s. 18 of the
Supreme Court Act
,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 444
.

[
2
]

Before commencing this action, the plaintiff
filed three similar statements of claim in Supreme Court and one statement of
claim in Provincial Court (Small Claims). The Supreme Court actions all stem
from an allegation that the RCMP implanted a microchip in his brain and a radio
frequency chip in his neck and that it uses these devices variously to monitor
and record the plaintiff’s thoughts, to control his thoughts and actions, and,
finally, to communicate with him.

[
3
]

The actions commenced by the plaintiff before
this action are as follows:

(1)       S53706:
Filed on June 26, 2008, in Nanaimo.

(2)       S55166: Filed on December 9, 2008, with an amended
statement of claim filed on March 20, 2009, in Nanaimo.

(3)       S55228: Filed on December 17, 2008, with an amended
statement of claim filed on March 20, 2009, in Nanaimo.

(4)       C56912: Filed on June 24, 2009, in the Nanaimo Provincial
Court (Small Claims).

[
4
]

On December 2, 2008, A.F. Wilson J. dismissed
the first action in its entirety under R. 19(24)(a)-(c):
Rose v. University
of British Columbia
,
2008 BCSC 1661
. He found that the claim was
bound to fail and disclosed no reasonable claim against any of the defendants
because, in general, the allegations did not specify by whom, when, where or
how the tortious acts were allegedly committed. Further, he concluded the
pleadings were frivolous, vexatious, embarrassing and prejudicial.

[
5
]

Halfyard J. struck out the second and third
actions and dismissed them as against all of the defendants on August 14, 2009:

Rose v. Canada (Royal Canadian Mounted Police)
,
2009 BCSC 1116
. Halfyard J. found the main allegations in the second action
consisted of or related to the same subject matter as in the first action. As
such, A.F. Wilson J.’s decision that the first action failed to disclose any
reasonable claim applied as an estoppel in respect of the defendants named in
both proceedings. There also was no reasonable claim against the newly named
defendants. Additionally, Halfyard J. found the second action was embarrassing.
He chose not to include a detailed analysis of the third action, but found that
the issues in both the second and third actions should have been raised in the
first action because they belonged to the same subject of litigation. As such,
both were vexatious and an abuse of the court process.

[
6
]

The plaintiff did not appeal either of these decisions, but
instead filed this action in the Victoria Registry on
September 30, 2009.

[
7
]

I need not set out the specific claims made in the previous three
Supreme Court statements of claim as they are fully set out in the decisions to
which I have referred. The essential allegations are unchanged from action to
action; the differences are found in the identification of the parties, the
language used, and the remedies that the plaintiff seeks. For example, the
plaintiff has used the terms “BCIsys [brain computer interface] System,” “brain
computer interface brain to brain network surveillance computer system [BCI-BTB
System],” “brain computer interface brain to brain communication surveillance
system,” and “two-tier Province of British Columbia/RCMP network computer
environment” or “computer environment” to refer to the alleged network used by
the RCMP. Regarding damages here, he seeks a broad range of damages including
non-pecuniary damages, past and future loss of income, aggravated damages and
punitive damages.  Additionally, the plaintiff asks the court to order the RCMP
and the governments of Canada and British Columbia to facilitate and pay for
the removal of his implant.

[
8
]

Although aware of the fourth action in
Provincial Court (Small Claims), Halfyard J. did not make any order respecting
it. There is an additional component to the Provincial Court action that I will
discuss later when I address the defendants’ application under s. 18 of the
Supreme
Court Act
.

[
9
]

Rule 19(24) states:

(24)      At any stage of a proceeding the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an
endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it discloses no reasonable claim or defence
as the case may be,

(b)        it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious,

(c)        it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair
trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)        it is otherwise an abuse of the process of
the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
10
]

The defendants rely on all four grounds in R.
19(24).

[
11
]

In a claim under R. 19(24)(a), the applicant
must show that it is “‘plain and obvious’ that the plaintiff’s statement of
claim discloses no reasonable cause of action,” assuming that the material
facts as pleaded in the statement of claim are true:
Hunt v. Carey Canada
Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, 74 D.L.R. (4th) 321 at para.
33
.

[
12
]

If the allegations in the plaintiff’s statement
of claim are viewed as true, they disclose, at a minimum, a cause of action in
tortious assault. The plaintiff’s statement of claim in this action, if read in
conjunction with his affidavit, is less general and speculative than his
statement of claim in the first action. With appropriate amendments respecting
time, place, the identification of individual tortfeasors, and vicarious
liability, it is arguable that the defendants have not met the test in
Hunt

respecting R. 19(24)(a).

[
13
]

The difficulty that remains, however, is that
the essential allegations are clearly fictional and cannot rationally be considered
true. While this might be addressed under R. 19(24)(a) on the basis that allegations
based on assumptions and speculations need not be taken as true (see
Operation
Dismantle Inc. v. The Queen
,
1985 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441 at 455, 18 D.L.R. (4th)
481), it is not necessary that I do so. There is ample room under the other
subrules to address the difficulty in this case.

[
14
]

In my view, the pleadings should be struck out
in their entirety on the grounds that it is plain and obvious that they are
frivolous, vexatious and an abuse of the process of the court contrary to R.
19(24)(b) and (d). Given my conclusions, it will not be necessary to consider
the defendants’ further arguments concerning R. 19(24)(c).

[
15
]

As stated by Master Baker in
Borsato v. Basra
,

2000 BCSC 28
, 43 C.P.C. (4th) 96, at para.
24
, “[a] pleading is frivolous if it
is without substance, groundless, fanciful, ‘trifles with the court’ or wastes
time.” That statement aptly describes the plaintiff’s essential allegations:
they are fanciful and incapable of proof.

[
16
]

In
Skender v. Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
, 289
D.L.R. (4th) 111, at para.
64
, the British Columbia Court of Appeal accepted
the various conditions that make a pleading vexatious as set out in
Re Lang
Michener and Fabian
(1987),
1987 CanLII 172 (ON HCJ)
, 59 O.R. (2d) 353 at 358-59, 37 D.L.R. (4th) 685
(H.C.J.). One is whether it is obvious that the action cannot succeed, as is
the case here.

[
17
]

The plaintiff submitted three articles to this
Court to support his claim that the alleged technology to read and control his
mind and to communicate with him by microchip exists. Two of the articles
appeared in legal journals: Ian R. Kerr, Max Binnie & Cynthia Aoki,
“Tessling on My Brain: The Future of Lie Detection and Brain Privacy in the
Criminal Justice System” (2008) 50 Canadian Journal of Criminology and Criminal
Justice 367; and Elaine M. Ramesh, “Time Enough? Consequences of Human
Microchip Implantation” (1997) 8 Risk: Health, Safety & Environment 373.

[
18
]

“Tessling on My Brain” describes imaging
technologies which allow brain waves to be externally and remotely measured.
Imaging devices do not yet have the ability to interface with implantable
microchips. The authors, at 376, also state:

If
neuro-imaging technologies really could scan the brain the way a computer scans
a hard drive, then there would be a strong argument in support of the claim
that brain scans are not meaningless since they would clearly reveal intimate
details about an individual’s life. However, this is not the current state of
the art. EEG scans merely determine whether information is recognized by the
subject and fMRI scans only pinpoint brain activity
;
neither can
actually read a person’s mind
in a way that WIRED magazine and other
popular culture sources would have us believe. [Emphasis added. Citations
omitted.]

Further, at 380, they assert that
surreptitious and remote brain scanning is a “far-off possibility.”

[
19
]

Ramesh, discussed the possibility of embedding
microchips, similar to those currently implanted in animals, into people to
read information, such as a person’s identification or medical history. She
noted, at 374, that this technology has “not yet been perfected,” although IBM
was working on “personal area network technology” to transfer data stored on a
human implant to another person or to an external mechanical system. Further,
the plaintiff has alleged that an implanted person can be tracked anywhere in
the world, but Ramesh points out at 385-86:

Microprocessor-based
implantable telemetry systems have been developed which require batteries for
power to emit signals. However, batteries present problems due to their
lifetimes and weight. These problems need to be addressed for implantable
microchips to have such [tracking] capabilities.

[
20
]

There is nothing in either article to support
the plaintiff’s theory that this technology would permit a third party to
somehow read or control a person’s thoughts or that the ability to transfer
this data from a distance exists. The third article does support the
plaintiff’s claims, but it is only available online from websites that are not
reputable. It has not been published in any accepted scientific, medical or
legal journal and would not meet the test in
R. v. Mohan
,
1994 CanLII 80 (SCC)
, [1994] 2
S.C.R. 9, 114 D.L.R. (4th) 419, for the admissibility of expert evidence or
novel scientific evidence.

[
21
]

There is, in my view, no rational possibility
that a court could accept that this technology exists now, let alone existed in
2003. The existence of the technology is a critical component of the
plaintiff’s claims. Therefore, his pleadings are groundless, fanciful, and cannot
succeed; to allow the claims to go forward would waste the court’s time since
it is inevitably doomed to failure.  No amendments to the pleadings could
remedy this defect. As such, the pleadings must be struck in their entirety.

[
22
]

Further, as set out in
Lang Michener
at
358,

vexatious proceedings exist when an action is brought “to determine
an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent
jurisdiction” and when grounds and issues that have been raised are “rolled
forward into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented.” Similarly, a
pleading can be classified as frivolous if it is obviously unsustainable because
of estoppel:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish
Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.), at para.
47
. A pleading is
an abuse of process when a party does not use the processes of court fairly and
a party’s claims violate principles such as “judicial economy, consistency,
finality and the integrity of the administration of justice”:
Dempsey v.
Envision Credit Union
,
2006 BCSC 750
, at paras.
9
, 12.

[
23
]

The plaintiff has repeated many of the claims
from his three previous Supreme Court actions in this action, although, as I
earlier observed, he has changed some of the language. For example, the
plaintiff has always alleged a breach of his
Charter
rights and this is
the third time he has sought damages for the possibility of a brain tumour. Two
previous judges have already dismissed these claims and the plaintiff is
estopped from proceeding with them. By repeatedly beginning new actions which
raise the same allegations and claims, rather than appealing the previous
decisions, the plaintiff is abusing the court process.

[
24
]

The only new claims concern the loss of brain
privacy and security, the violation of the plaintiff’s rights as a First
Nations Indian, and the request that the defendants facilitate and pay for an
operation to have the microchip removed. However, these claims are still based
on the same circumstances and subject matter as in the prior actions. Thus, these
new claims should have been raised in the earlier proceedings.

[
25
]

Therefore, I order that the pleadings be struck
and the action be dismissed as against all defendants.

[
26
]

Section 18 of the
Supreme Court Act

reads:

18.       If,
on application by any person, the court is satisfied that a person has
habitually, persistently and without reasonable grounds, instituted vexatious
legal proceedings in Supreme Court or in the Provincial Court against the same
or different persons, the court may, after hearing that person or giving him or
her an opportunity to be heard, order that a legal proceeding must not, without
leave of the court, be instituted by that person in any court.

[
27
]

According to
British Columbia (Public
Guardian and Trustee) v. Brown
,
2002 BCSC 1152
, at paras.
47-48
,

the
applicants must establish two elements in order to be successful:

(1)       The proceedings must be “vexatious”; in other words, they
are annoying, irritating, distressing or harassing and are taken without
reasonable grounds; and

(2)       Considered objectively, there must be a knowing and
deliberate repetition or continuation of the vexatious conduct.

[
28
]

In determining whether proceedings are
vexatious, it is also necessary to consider “the whole history of the matter”
and whether the person instituting the proceedings has failed to pay the costs
of unsuccessful proceedings:
Lang Michener
at 358-59.

[
29
]

Two previous judges and I have all found the
plaintiff’s Supreme Court actions concerning this matter vexatious. Further,
the plaintiff has not paid any of the costs orders from the two previous
judgments.

[
30
]

I accept that the plaintiff likely believes the
allegations he makes and does not see his actions as vexatious. However, it is
not necessary that the plaintiff knows that his conduct is vexatious. The
plaintiff has filed these four actions over the course of 15 months. The
plaintiff commenced this action after assuring Halfyard J. on July 23, 2009,
that he would not file another action regarding the same issues until a s. 18
application could be heard. After reading Halfyard J.’s judgment, the plaintiff
ought to have known that this action would also be considered vexatious since
it was based on similar subject matter with similar claims and could not
succeed for that reason alone.  Instead, the plaintiff has knowingly and
intentionally repeated his vexatious conduct. He has habitually, persistently
and without reasonable grounds started legal proceedings against the
applicants.

[
31
]

In my opinion, if I do not grant the s. 18
order, it is highly likely that the plaintiff will continue to file statements
of claim that are derived from the same allegations as those that have already
been dismissed. This would require these defendants, and possibly others, to
spend time and money defending these vexatious pleadings. Although a s. 18
order is a drastic measure, here it is necessary to ensure the proper
administration of justice.

[
32
]

The defendants also ask that the s. 18 order
apply to the plaintiff continuing any legal actions. In
Kaiser (Re)
,

2008 BCSC 451
, 41 C.B.R. (5th) 200, at paras.
19‑20
,
Chamberlist J. noted that a s.18 order should not apply to unrelated legal
proceedings that were commenced prior to the s. 18 order in the absence of
express terms being included in the order.

[
33
]

With these pleadings dismissed, it appears that
the plaintiff’s only outstanding action is the one in Provincial Court (Small
Claims) against Her Majesty the Queen in right of the Province of British
Columbia, the Attorney General of British Columbia, the Solicitor General of
British Columbia, and the Nanaimo Provincial Court Sheriff’s Department.

[
34
]

The claims in the Small Claims Court action stem
from physical injuries, one of which the plaintiff alleges occurred due to a
defective door at the RCMP station, and the second which the plaintiff alleges
was a result of the negligence and subsequent actions of the Sheriff’s
Department. While the plaintiff does, once again, mention cognitive
manipulation in his pleadings, the bulk of the claim appears unrelated. I am
not prepared to extend the s. 18 order to prohibit the plaintiff continuing the
Small Claims Court action.  A Provincial Court judge, during a settlement
conference or other Small Claims Court proceeding, can determine which portions
of the pleading falls under issue estoppel or should otherwise be struck.

[
35
]

In conclusion, I grant the s. 18 order: The
plaintiff must not, without leave of this court, institute a legal proceeding
in any court of British Columbia. This order does not apply to the Provincial
Court (Small Claims) action which the plaintiff has already started. If the
plaintiff has already commenced any other proceeding, but not yet served it
upon the defendants, the defendants have leave to apply to extend the s. 18
order to such a proceeding.

[
36
]

In summary, I strike out the statement of claim
and dismiss the proceeding as against all defendants. I grant the s. 18 order
on the terms set out above. The defendants are entitled to costs on
Scale B.

“M.D.
Macualay,
J.”

The
Honourable Mr. Justice Macaulay
